title: Why a Dog's Nose Works in Stereo
central_question: How does a dog's nose separate smelling from breathing?
central_fact: A computer model built from MRI scans showed that a dog's nasal airflow splits into separate olfactory and respiratory paths, and each nostril samples a spatially separate patch of air.
takeaway: A dog's nose is a routing system as well as a sensor; its shape helps scent reach the olfactory region and may support comparing samples from two nostrils.

hook.text: A dog's nose splits air into two jobs.

scenes.narration: A dog's nose splits air into two jobs.

visual.description: A black Labrador mix with a graying muzzle lowers its nose to a fallen leaf on a garden path. The camera frames the snout and one relaxed eye, with soft green foliage blurred behind. The dog sniffs calmly and lifts its head slightly.
visual.subject: one black Labrador mix with a graying muzzle and a glossy black nose
visual.motion: slow push-in as the dog sniffs the leaf
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, nose in the lower middle third, eye on the upper-third line
visual.continuity: same black dog, red collar, and garden path in every scene

scenes.narration: When a dog sniffs, air does not take one simple path through the nose. It splits.

visual.description: The same black dog holds its nose close to the leaf while two faint, translucent ribbons of air curl toward the nostrils. One ribbon rises along the upper snout, the other runs lower. The dog stays still and curious, and the garden light is soft.
visual.shot_type: macro three-quarter view of the snout
visual.subject: the same black dog's nose and muzzle, with two abstract airflow ribbons
visual.motion: very slow lateral drift; the ribbons divide and settle
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, nostrils centered, ribbons flowing into the upper and lower thirds
visual.continuity: same glossy nose, graying muzzle, and red collar edge

scenes.narration: A 2010 study built a computer model of a dog's nasal airway from MRI scans.

visual.description: A translucent, glass-like model of a dog's head rotates slowly above a dark studio surface. The snout is anatomically correct, and a soft amber light suggests the internal nasal airway without opening the body. No labels or readable marks appear.
visual.subject: one translucent canine head model with a detailed snout
visual.motion: slow orbital rotation, then a gentle hold
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, model centered with generous dark negative space
visual.continuity: same amber palette and dark background throughout the model sequence

scenes.narration: The simulation showed two separate flows: one for breathing, and one that carries odor molecules to the olfactory region.

visual.description: An abstract view of two smooth ribbons of light moving through a dark amber space. The upper ribbon curves toward the rear and slows into a fine mesh; the lower ribbon runs straighter and wider toward the throat. The shapes are non-literal and unlabeled.
visual.subject: two separate airflow ribbons, one high and narrow, one low and broad
visual.motion: slow forward drift; the upper ribbon spreads into a delicate mesh
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, both ribbons centered with clear separation
visual.continuity: same amber palette, grain, and dark background as the model scene

scenes.narration: Each nostril also draws from its own patch of air, because the nose's reach is smaller than the gap between the nostrils.

visual.description: A front macro view of the same black dog's nose. Two separate pale ribbons curl in from different directions, one toward each nostril, with a clear gap between them. The muzzle is relaxed and the whiskers are still.
visual.subject: the same black dog's two nostrils and muzzle, with two separate air ribbons
visual.motion: static camera; the ribbons pulse gently inward
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, nose centered, one ribbon entering from each side
visual.continuity: same glossy nose, graying muzzle, and red collar edge

scenes.narration: That may help a dog compare scent strength on each side. The nose is a routing system, not just a detector. Its shape helps scent reach the receptors.

visual.description: The same black dog stands on the garden path beside an owner's open hand, nose lifted toward a light breeze. The dog's posture is relaxed and its tail is loose. The camera pulls back slowly to reveal the green garden, then fades.
visual.subject: the same black dog and an owner's open hand
visual.motion: slow pull-back; the dog lifts its nose and holds
visual.framing: vertical 9:16, dog in the lower middle third, open garden above
visual.continuity: same dog, red collar, garden path, and soft daylight; no other animals

claims.text: Seven dogs weighing 6.8-52.9 kg were trained to sniff while wearing a flow-measuring muzzle; their sniff frequency was 4-7 Hz.
claims.limits: Seven dogs is a small sample, and the muzzle was a specialized measurement device rather than a natural tracking setup.

claims.text: The computational model was reconstructed from high-resolution MRI scans of the left nasal airway of a 29.5 kg female Labrador retriever mixed-breed dog.
claims.limits: The model represents one dog's anatomy and is described by the authors as generally representative of a mesaticephalic canine nasal cavity.

claims.text: The simulation showed separate olfactory and respiratory airflow paths; in the modeled relaxed, undilated nostril case, about 12-13% of inspired air reached the chemosensory region.
claims.limits: The percentage comes from a simulation with a relaxed nostril; the authors note that realistic nostril motion could change it.

claims.text: At peak inspiration, each nostril's reach was about 1 cm, smaller than the separation between the nostrils, yielding spatially separate air samples that may support bilateral comparison and odor source localization.
claims.limits: The bilateral comparison and localization functions are proposed interpretations, not direct behavioral measurements in this study.

claims.text: The expiratory jet was directed ventrolaterally, which the authors propose can mix nearby odorants and reduce blow-off directly ahead of the nostril.
claims.limits: The expiratory flow was modeled and described qualitatively; the mixing benefit is an interpretation of the airflow pattern.

claims.text: The study proposes that nasal airflow architecture helps explain canine olfactory acuity, but it does not show that airflow alone accounts for every difference between dogs and other species.
claims.limits: The study combines flow measurements and a single anatomical model; it does not test all possible contributors to olfactory performance.

visual_policy.style: Observational real-footage montage built from third-party pet clips, natural light, calm pacing, and species-correct behavior.
visual_policy.anatomy: Every animal must be species-correct and anatomically coherent. Multiple individuals may appear across clips; reject malformed, uncanny, or merged animals.
visual_policy.welfare: The dog is calm, curious, and unrestrained in a quiet garden. No leash jerking, force, injury, or distress. The model sequence contains no dissection or animal tissue. Reject any clip with staged distress, restraint, injury, aggression, or a visible watermark.
visual_policy.continuity: Keep the question, tone, and caption position consistent across clips. Do not imply that different animals are the same individual. Avoid repeated or watermarked clips.
visual_policy.disclosure: Real-footage montage using third-party clips for illustration; not documentary footage or scientific evidence.

notes: The stereo-sampling and airflow-routing functions are proposed explanations, not a complete account of canine scent ability.
Do not show dissection or imply that the translucent model is a real specimen.

risk_notes: The CFD model is based on one dog's anatomy; avoid presenting its percentages as universal canine values.
Do not claim dogs smell in 'stereo' exactly like human hearing; the video uses stereo as a metaphor for two spatially separate samples.
